t.3.1: Leaving the other gods, the thousand eyes of Maghavan fell all at once upon him; for, depending on what purpose they need served, the regard of the mighty toward those who depend on them is usually fickle.
t.3.2: He, granted by Vāsava a place close beside his own seat with the words “Sit here,” welcomed his master's favor with a bow of his head and began to speak to him privately thus.
t.3.3: Command me, you who know the distinctive worth of men: what is there in the worlds that must be done for you? I wish this favor of yours, which has shown itself in your remembering me, to be enhanced by your command.
t.3.4: By whom, coveting your station, has jealousy been roused in you through exceedingly prolonged austerities? He shall straightway become subject to the command of this bow of mine, on which the arrow is already set.
t.3.5: Who is it, not approved by you, that has taken to the path of liberation out of fear of the torment of rebirth? Let him remain long bound by the sidelong glances of beautiful women, made skilful by their gracefully arched brows.
t.3.6: Tell me, which enemy of yours, even one taught statecraft by Uśanas himself, shall I, having sent passion ahead as my secret agent, assail in both his wealth and his dharma, as a swollen flood assails the two banks of a river?
t.3.7: Which full-hipped woman, bound to the hard vow of faithfulness to a single husband, who has entered your restless mind through her loveliness, do you wish to have cast off her modesty and cling with her arms about your neck in an embrace of her own seeking?
t.3.8: O lover, by what wrathful woman have you been spurned, though you bowed at her feet, because of some offense in lovemaking? I shall make her body, stricken with deep remorse, seek refuge on a bed of tender shoots.
t.3.10: By your grace, though my only weapons are flowers, with Madhu alone as my companion I could shake the composure even of Hara, who bears the Pināka in his hand; what are other bowmen to me?
t.3.9: Be gracious, O hero, and let your thunderbolt rest: which enemy of the gods, the might of his arms made futile by my arrows, shall tremble even before women whose lips quiver with anger?
t.3.11: Then Ākhaṇḍala lowered his foot from his thigh, so that the footstool was honored by its tread, and spoke these words to Kāma, who had revealed his own power for the purpose they had in mind.
t.3.12: Friend, all this is fitting in you: I have two weapons, the thunderbolt and you. The thunderbolt is blunted against those mighty in the power of their austerities, but you are a weapon that reaches everywhere and accomplishes its aim.
t.3.13: I know your strength, and so I shall appoint you, as one equal to myself, to a weighty task. Kṛṣṇa, seeing that Śeṣa is able to bear the earth, assigns him the task of bearing his own body.
t.3.14: Since you have wished for your arrows to find their way to the bull-marked god, our task is as good as accomplished by you. Know now that this alone is what is desired by the sharers of the sacrificial portions, whose enemies have grown mighty.
t.3.16: Strive to make the devout daughter of the Snow Mountain pleasing to him whose self is restrained; for among women she alone is fit to be the field in which his seed is sown, so Ātmabhū has instructed.
t.3.15: For these gods desire, for their victory, a general sprung from the seed of Bhava; and he, born from Brahmā's body, his self fixed in Brahman, can be won by the fall of a single arrow of yours.
t.3.17: And by her father's command the daughter of the lord of mountains waits upon Sthāṇu as he practices austerities on the mountain plateau. This I have heard from the mouths of the Apsarases, for that band serves as my spy.
t.3.18: So go, and for its success accomplish this task of the gods. This aim can be brought about only through another cause, and it needs you as its supreme auxiliary cause, just as the sprout within a seed needs water before it can emerge.
t.3.19: In that means of victory for the gods, the reach of a weapon is indeed yours alone; you are fortunate. For a deed shared with no one else, even if it is not renowned, brings fame to men.
t.3.20: These gods are your petitioners, and the task is one for all three worlds; your work is done with the bow, and is not overly cruel. Ah, how enviable is your valor!
t.3.21: And this Madhu, O Manmatha, because of his constant companionship with you, is your helper even without being asked; for who ever commands the wind, saying, "Be the kindler of the fire"?
t.3.22: Saying "So be it," Madana received his master's command upon his head, as one receives a blessed garland left from worship, and set out; and Indra touched his body with a hand made rough from patting Airāvata.
t.3.23: Followed by his beloved friend Mādhava and, with apprehension, by Rati, he, who sought success in his task even at the cost of his own body, went to the Himalayan hermitage of Sthāṇu.
t.3.24: In that forest, Madhu, working against the ascetic concentration of the self-restrained sages, made himself the very embodiment of the pride of the mind-born god of love and spread forth in full bloom.
t.3.25: When the hot-rayed sun set out toward the quarter guarded by Kubera, the southern quarter, overstepping the appointed season, released from her mouth the fragrant breeze, as though it were a sigh of wounded grief.
t.3.26: At once the aśoka tree brought forth blossoms together with tender shoots, starting right from its trunk; it did not wait for the touch of lovely women's feet with their jingling anklets.
t.3.27: When the new mango-blossom arrow, its feathers lovely with the sprouting of tender shoots, had been brought to completion, Madhu at once set bees upon it, like the letters of Manobhava's name.
t.3.29: Curved like the crescent moon because they had not yet opened, the deep-red palāśa blossoms shone like fresh nail-marks on the woodland glades just united with Vasanta.
t.3.28: Though its color was of the highest beauty, the heart grieved over the karṇikāra for its lack of fragrance; for as a rule the working of the Creator of the universe turns away from bringing all excellences together in one.
t.3.30: The splendor of Spring, displaying on her face a tilaka-blossom adorned with clinging bees like painted lines of collyrium, adorned the lip of the mango's young shoots with a hue as soft as the early dawn.
t.3.31: The deer, their glances hindered by grains of pollen from the blossom-clusters of the priyāla trees, roamed wild with passion against the wind through the woodland glades, where rustling leaves were falling.
t.3.32: The sweet song that the male cuckoo sang, his throat made husky by tasting the mango shoots, became the very speech of Smara, skilled at breaking down the pride of indignant women.
t.3.33: With the passing of the frost, the lips of the Kiṃpuruṣa women became clear and the complexion of their faces turned pale, and a rising of sweat set its foot upon the leaf-patterns painted on their faces.
t.3.34: The ascetics dwelling in Sthāṇu's forest, seeing that untimely onset of spring, only with difficulty remained masters of their minds, whose stirrings they held in check through strenuous effort.
t.3.35: When Madana, his flower-bow strung and Rati at his side, had come to that place, the mated pairs revealed through their actions a feeling steeped in the essence of love that had reached its utmost height.
t.3.36: The bee, following his own beloved, drank honey from a single flower-cup, and the black antelope scratched with his horn the doe, whose eyes were closed at his touch.
t.3.37: Out of love, the she-elephant gave her mate a trunkful of water fragrant with lotus pollen, and the cakravāka bird, whose name is that of a chariot's wheel, honored his wife with a half-eaten lotus stalk.
t.3.38: In the pauses between songs, the Kiṃpuruṣa kissed the face of his beloved, its painted leaf-designs slightly loosened by drops of the sweat of exertion, and lovely with eyes rolling from the flower-wine.
t.3.39: Even the trees received the embraces of bending branch-arms from their creeper-brides, whose breasts were ample clusters of blossoms and who were enchanting with lips of quivering young shoots.
t.3.41: Then Nandī, having gone to the doorway of the bower of creepers, a golden staff resting upon his left forearm, restrained the Gaṇas merely by the sign of a single finger laid upon his lips, as if to say, "No restlessness!"
t.3.40: Even though he heard the singing of the Apsarases at that moment, Hara remained intent on his meditation; for obstacles are never able to break the concentration of those who are masters of themselves.
t.3.42: At his command the entire forest, its trees unmoving, its bees hushed, its birds mute, and the roaming of its deer stilled, stood as though all its activity had been set down in a painting.
t.3.43: Avoiding the range of his glance, as one setting out on a journey avoids having Śukra before him, Kāma entered the place of meditation of the Lord of Beings, whose borders were enclosed by the interlocking branches of nameru trees.
t.3.44: He, whose bodily destruction was close at hand, saw the self-restrained Tryambaka seated upon an altar beneath a devadāru tree, spread with a covering of tiger skin.
t.3.45: He sat with the front of his body held steady in the paryaṅka posture, upright and erect, both shoulders gently lowered, and with his two hands laid palms upward, a full-blown lotus seemed to rest in the middle of his lap.
t.3.46: Him, whose mass of matted locks was bound up with serpents, on whose ear hung a doubled string of rudrākṣa beads, and who wore a knotted black antelope skin made all the darker by contact with the dark radiance of his throat.
t.3.47: With eyes whose fierce pupils were still and only faintly shining, which had ceased all play of the brows, whose rows of lashes did not quiver, and whose rays, cast downward, made the tip of his nose their target, he sat in meditation.
t.3.48: Through the restraint of the vital winds moving within him, he was like a rain-cloud without the agitation of rain, like a reservoir of waters without a wave, like a lamp burning unflickering where no wind blows.
t.3.49: With sprouts of light that rose from his head, having found their way out through the opening of the eye in his forehead, he was dimming the loveliness of the young crescent moon, whose delicacy surpassed even that of a lotus-stalk fiber.
t.3.51: Smara, seeing from close by the odd-eyed one in such a state, unassailable even by the mind, his hands gone limp with fear, did not notice that his arrow, and even his bow, had slipped from his own hand.
t.3.50: Him who, having settled in his heart his mind, its workings barred from the nine gates and made obedient through deep meditation, was beholding within himself that Self whom the knowers of the field know as the Imperishable.
t.3.52: Then the daughter of the king of mountains was seen, followed by two goddesses of the forest, as if rekindling with the excellence of her beauty his virile energy, which had all but been extinguished.
t.3.53: She came wearing an adornment of spring flowers, in which aśoka blossoms put rubies to shame, karṇikāras had drawn to themselves the luster of gold, and sinduvāra blossoms served as strings of pearls.
t.3.55: Again and again she held up her girdle of kesara flowers as it slipped from her hips, a girdle that seemed like a second bowstring for his bow, entrusted to her keeping by Smara, who knew the proper place for it.
t.3.54: Bent slightly, as it were, by the weight of her breasts, and wearing a garment the color of the young sun, she seemed a moving creeper rich with tender shoots, bowed down by its full clusters of blossoms.
t.3.56: Her eyes darting restlessly in alarm, she kept warding off with her play-lotus, moment after moment, the bee that hovered near her bimba-red lower lip, its thirst heightened by her fragrant breath.
t.3.57: Seeing her, flawless in every limb and a cause of shame even to Rati, the flower-bowed god once more hoped to accomplish his task with the trident-bearer, though Śiva had conquered his senses.
t.3.58: Umā arrived at the doorway of Śambhu, her husband-to-be, and just then he, having beheld within himself the supreme light called the Supreme Self, withdrew from his yoga.
t.3.59: Then the Lord, the ground beneath whom was held up only with difficulty from below by the tips of the serpent king's hoods, slowly released his breath and broke his firm cross-legged posture.
t.3.60: Bowing low, Nandī announced to him that the daughter of the Mountain had come to serve him, and he led her in, her entry granted by no more than a flick of the master's eyebrow.
t.3.61: After first bowing low, her two friends scattered at the feet of Tryambaka a heap of flowers of the season when winter ends, plucked by their own hands and interspersed with broken sprigs of tender leaves.
t.3.63: "May you win a husband who loves no other woman": so Bhava addressed her, and he spoke only the truth. For the words of the great lords never yield in this world a meaning contrary to what they say.
t.3.62: Umā too, letting slip the fresh karṇikāra blossom that shone amid her dark locks, bowed her head, from which the sprig at her ear had fallen, in obeisance to Vṛṣabhadhvaja.
t.3.65: Then Gaurī, with her copper-bright hand, offered to Giriśa, the ascetic, a rosary of lotus seeds from the Mandākinī, dried by the rays of the sun.
t.3.64: But Kāma, waiting for the right moment to loose his arrow and, like a moth, eager to enter the mouth of the fire, fixed Hara as his target in Umā's presence and fingered his bowstring again and again.
t.3.66: Because he holds dear those who love him, the Three-eyed One began to receive her; and at that moment the Flower-bowed One set upon his bow the unfailing arrow named Sammohana.
t.3.67: But Hara, his composure somewhat shaken, like the ocean at the first rising of the moon, cast his eyes upon Umā's face, with its lower lip red as the bimba fruit.
t.3.69: Then the Odd-Eyed One, once more forcibly restraining the agitation of his senses through his self-mastery, and wishing to see the cause of his own mind's disturbance, cast his gaze toward the edges of the quarters.
t.3.68: Śailasutā, too, revealing her feeling through limbs like young kadamba blossoms bursting into bloom, stood turned aside, with a face made all the lovelier by its eyes cast askance.
t.3.70: He saw Ātmayoni rising up to strike, his fist set at the outer corner of his right eye, his shoulder bent, his left foot drawn back, and his lovely bow drawn into a circle.
t.3.71: From the third eye of him, whose wrath had swelled at the assault upon his austerity and whose face was dreadful to behold with its knitted brows, a flashing fire with upward-leaping flames suddenly burst forth, so it is said.
t.3.72: Even while the cries of the gods, "Restrain your anger, O Lord, restrain it!", were still moving through the sky, that fire born from the eye of Bhava reduced Madana to a mere remnant of ashes.
t.3.73: Through a swoon born of the violent shock, which stilled the workings of her senses, Rati for a moment did not know of her husband's calamity, and so was, as it were, granted a kindness.
t.3.74: Having swiftly shattered that obstacle to his penance, as the thunderbolt shatters a great tree, the ascetic Bhūtapati, wishing to avoid the nearness of women, vanished together with his Bhūtas.
t.3.75: The daughter of the mountain, too, concluding that the longing of her lofty-headed father had come to nothing, and her own graceful body as well, and that this had happened before the eyes of her two friends, felt her shame grow all the greater; and, desolate, she somehow made her way toward home.
t.3.76: At once the Mountain lifted in his arms his pitiable daughter, whose eyes were closed in fear of Rudra's fury, and, like the elephant of the gods carrying a lotus plant caught on its tusks, he turned back along the path, his body stretched long by his speed.
